title: Heat Pumps are Not Hard: Here's what it will take to start pumping
summary: Explainer on heat pump system types and retrofit barriers in the US: insulate first, central AC homes are nearly ready, cheap gas kept US heat pumps mediocre, and installers inflate quotes.

assertions.quote: Heat pumps move heat rather than create it.

verdicts.note: Air-source heat pumps routinely deliver two to four units of heat per unit of electricity, as rated and field-measured COPs show.

assertions.quote: The wisest thing we can do in the short term can be expressed in these three simple words: insulate, insulate, and insulate.

verdicts.note: Reducing heat loss lowers the required heat pump size and running cost; DOE and retrofit programs recommend envelope work first, though it is not strictly required.

assertions.quote: Locally we need a consistent COP of 4 just to break even with the cost of gas

verdicts.note: Running cost versus gas is set by the electricity-to-gas price ratio divided by the seasonal COP, so local prices dominate the comparison.

Bill savings are very sensitive to prices (2019 elec-to-gas ratio 4.1 cuts gas homes with positive savings from 32-92% to 22-83%), but the range itself shows equipment efficiency matters as much as prices, so 'mainly prices' overstates.
EIA-derived break-even seasonal COP equals the electricity-to-gas price ratio times furnace AFUE, so the outcome depends on local prices and on the heat pump's seasonal efficiency together.

Edwards finds large regional differences in heat pump operating costs that depend on local climate as well as the price of electricity relative to gas, so prices are a main driver but not the only one.

LBNL retrofit database (1,739 projects): about 70 electrification projects in states with high electricity costs raised household energy costs, and the authors conclude savings must be judged state by state given the variation in gas and electricity prices.

The report maps electricity and fuel prices against the outdoor temperature above which a mini-split is cheaper than fuel heat; the answer turns on the price pair and on the unit's efficiency at that temperature, and at 2015-16 New England prices gas won almost everywhere.

In the UK, total energy use fell 40% after switching from a gas boiler, yet running costs came out slightly higher because electricity costs more per kWh than gas, which shows prices decide the comparison (one country, one set of prices).

Advocacy-adjacent Canadian lifetime-cost model (five cities): regional energy prices and climate are the biggest drivers of whether heat pumps beat gas, with prices and climate both mattering (e.g. low-gas-price, cold Edmonton vs Montreal and Halifax).

assertions.quote: I cannot see the quote he got as anything but a dishonest company taking advantage of someone looking to install a “trendy” heat pump

verdicts.note: Installed heat pump prices are high and opaque relative to equipment cost, but evidence on systematic markups beyond labor, permits and overhead is mostly anecdotal.

Wholesale heat pumps cost only $200-$500 more than equivalent ACs yet installs often cost more, partly because larger capacity and wiring are needed and partly because inexperienced installers may charge more to cover hassle and risk; no measure of markup over cost.

LBNL cites gross margins (overhead plus profit) averaging 47% of energy upgrade project costs, so materials, labor and equipment are roughly half of the total; this is business overhead, not proof of overcharging.

assertions.quote: homes with central air conditioning are basically already set.

verdicts.note: Ducted heat pumps commonly replace a central AC condenser and coil on existing ducts, though some duct systems need changes.
Ducted heat pumps connected to existing duct systems are described as the typical case, with the caveat that existing duct airflow may force undersizing and more backup heat.
The ducted heat pumps' indoor coils were installed in the homes' existing furnace ductwork, like a traditional AC coil, using the furnace fan to distribute heat.
Ducted cold-climate heat pumps replaced furnaces at 21 sites; 71% needed no major duct upgrades (though 76% needed minor ones), so existing ductwork was mostly reused.

assertions.quote: Because, once again, air conditioners ARE heat pumps!

verdicts.note: An air-source heat pump is a vapor-compression air conditioner with a reversing valve and defrost controls.

assertions.quote: airflow may become a challenge in existing homes thanks to ductwork restrictions.

verdicts.note: Heat pumps supply cooler air than furnaces and need more airflow per unit of heat, so ducts sized for a furnace or a smaller AC can restrict them.

assertions.quote: Around here they all seem to be oversized by a factor of about 2.

verdicts.note: Field studies of US residential HVAC commonly find furnaces and ACs sized well above calculated design loads.
The authors cite overly conservative equipment sizing as a cause of high upfront costs to be addressed with sizing guidance, without measuring how common it is.

LBNL: fuel-fired heating equipment was sized far larger (typically 356 ft2 per ton) than heat pumps or air conditioners (543 and 555 ft2 per ton), suggesting generous furnace sizing, while many heat pumps were sized aggressively small; no load calculations were compared.

Heating-load audits found the heat pumps at Sites 5 and 8 very undersized (under 40% of design load) and Sites 10, 11 and 13 also undersized; oversizing was the exception in this 12-site northwest sample.

Program mini-splits averaged about 2.1-2.6 times the Manual J cooling load of the spaces they served, but for heating nearly half were undersized, so the oversizing was one-directional and probably came from sizing to heating.

The furnaces being replaced (mostly 66-100 kBtu/h gas) tended to be well above the homes' Manual J heating loads, so the cold-climate heat pumps installed were much smaller; this covers 21 sites and furnaces only.
In the German field trial many heat pumps were oversized relative to consumption, with very high switching frequencies in some; a heat pump sample in Germany, not HVAC contractors generally.

assertions.quote: the performance challenges heat pumps currently encounter at very cold temperatures

verdicts.note: Air-source heat pump COP and maximum output both decline as outdoor temperature falls, as manufacturer and NEEP data show.
Heat pump efficiency falls with ambient temperature, and at low temperatures the load can exceed capacity so the model falls back to resistance heat (COP 1).
Capacity retention curves from lab and NEEP manufacturer data fall from 100% of rated output at 47F to 47% (single-speed) or 85% (cold-climate) at 5F.
The cold-climate Mitsubishi unit RMI models has a COP at max capacity that falls from 3.5 at 47F to 2.1 at 17F and 1.4 at -13F; the report shows efficiency falling but gives no capacity figures.

Edwards fits heat pump COP from the NEEP database as a linear function of outdoor temperature (COP = 0.05T + 1.6 above 5F), with single-stage units dropping to about COP 1 below 5F; the source covers efficiency only, not capacity.
A 1-ton ductless unit in northern Minnesota held its median capacity from 10F to -15F but delivered only about 2,600 Btu/h (about 20% of its rated 5F capacity) between -20F and -25F.
Measured heat-pump-only cycles averaged COP about 1.3 at the 10F change point rising to 3.0-4.5 at 50-60F; outdoor temperature had the largest effect on COP across six Minnesota sites.

The evaluation states unit efficiency drops as outdoor temperature drops and estimates from manufacturer data that capacity falls about 20% from 17 F to 5 F at fixed airflow; about half the units could not meet the space heating load below 17 F.

Heating COPs rose steadily with outdoor temperature (median 1.6 in the cold bins up to about 5.2), and the report notes conventional heat pumps lose capacity below 40 F and keep only a fraction in the teens.
Older heat pumps lose efficiency in colder temperatures, less so for newer models; the passage says nothing about capacity.
Across the UK trial the measured COP fell as outdoor temperature fell, to a median 2.44 on the coldest day (mean -0.4C) against a seasonal 2.80; capacity was not reported.
Metered COP across 166 units in Maine fell as the outdoor temperature dropped, averaging 2 at -10F against a season average of 3.15.

assertions.quote: Whatever savings the rebate might bring can simply evaporate if the installer builds it into the quote

verdicts.note: Studies of energy-efficiency subsidies find some pass-through to sellers, but most rebate value usually reaches buyers.
